title: What is a linked list — a chain of nodes, each node holds data + a pointer to the next node; unlike array, nodes are NOT stored side by side in memory.

s1_definition.profdef: A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node stores a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is accessed through a head reference to the first node, and the last node points to null. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored in contiguous memory; they can live anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references.

The slips are scattered in different drawers, but each one tells you where the next one is. You start from the first slip (the head) and follow the arrows until you reach a slip whose arrow points to nothing, which is the end.
s1_definition.oneliner: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next, connected by references rather than by sitting side by side in memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node stores a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is accessed through a head reference to the first node, and the last node points to null. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored in contiguous memory; they can live anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a chain of pending transactions for Rajesh. Each transaction slip has the transaction details plus an arrow pointing to the next slip. The slips are scattered in different drawers, but each one tells you where the next one is. You start from the first slip (the head) and follow the arrows until you reach a slip whose arrow points to nothing, which is the end.

**One line to remember:** A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next, connected by references rather than by sitting side by side in memory.

sections.s2_technical:
A node is a small object with two parts: the data it carries, and a `next` reference to the following node. The list itself usually holds only a `head` reference, which points to the first node. To reach any node you start at the head and follow next references one by one. The final node's next is null, which signals the end.

The defining contrast with an array is memory layout. An array stores its elements in one continuous block, so element `i` is found instantly by computing an address offset, giving O(1) random access. A linked list stores nodes anywhere on the heap, so to reach the fifth node you must walk through the first four, giving O(n) access. The trade-off is that inserting or deleting at the front of a linked list is O(1) because you just re-point a reference, whereas inserting at the front of an array is O(n) because every element must shift.

In Java you rarely write your own linked list for application code because `java.util.LinkedList` exists, but understanding the structure matters for interviews and for problems like reversing a list or detecting a cycle. A singly linked list has one next pointer per node; a doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so you can walk backwards, which is how `java.util.LinkedList` is actually implemented. A senior nuance is that linked lists have poor cache locality because nodes are scattered, so for pure iteration an ArrayList is usually faster in practice despite the same big-O.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes Rajesh's pending transactions in the order they arrived, and new transactions are frequently added. A linked list models this chain of pending slips, where each slip points to the next. This is exactly what a linked list is — a chain of nodes connected by next references.

Problem 2 — We need to add a new pending transaction quickly at the front of the chain without shifting everything. This is exactly why a linked list is useful: inserting at the head is a constant-time pointer change.

The code has a `TransactionNode` class holding an amount and a next reference, and a `PendingTransactions` class with `addFront` and `printAll`. The demo builds a small chain and walks it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three addFront calls with 1000, 2000, then 3000.

Step 1 — addFront(1000): a new node with 1000 is created, its next is null (head was null), and head now points to it. Chain: 1000.

Step 2 — addFront(2000): a new node with 2000 is created, its next points to the 1000 node, and head moves to the 2000 node. Chain: 2000 then 1000.

Step 3 — addFront(3000): a new node with 3000 is created, its next points to the 2000 node, and head moves to the 3000 node. Chain: 3000 then 2000 then 1000.

Step 4 — printAll starts at head (3000) and follows next references, printing 3000, then 2000, then 1000, then reaching null and stopping. Because we always inserted at the front, the newest is first.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Pending transactions (head to tail):
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.3000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.2000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.1000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  addFront(1000): head → [1000|next=null]
  addFront(2000): head → [2000|next] → [1000|null]
  addFront(3000): head → [3000|next] → [2000|next] → [1000|null]
    │
    ▼
  printAll() traversal:
  head → 3000 → 2000 → 1000 → null
         print   print  print   stop
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is reached through a head reference to the first node, and the very last node points to null to mark the end. The defining characteristic, compared with an array, is that the nodes are not stored side by side in memory; they can sit anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references, so I follow the chain by starting at the head and hopping from one node to the next.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used a linked chain to model Rajesh's pending transactions, where each pending slip points to the next one. New transactions arrive constantly, and I add them at the front of the chain, which is a constant-time operation because I simply create a new node, point it at the current head, and move the head to the new node. Nothing else has to shift.

The trade-off I always explain is access versus modification. Reaching the fifth node means walking through the first four, so random access is linear time, whereas an array gives constant-time access by index. In exchange, inserting or deleting at the front of a linked list is constant time, while doing the same in an array forces every later element to shift. I also mention that linked lists have poor cache locality because the nodes are scattered in memory, so for pure iteration an ArrayList is often faster in practice even though the big-O looks similar, and that Java's own LinkedList is actually a doubly linked list with a previous pointer as well so it can be traversed in both directions.
